title: Analytic Function Theory Perspective on Newton's Binomial Theorem
content: This file approaches Newton's generalized binomial theorem through the lens of analytic function theory. Instead of proving convergence directly, it shows that the ODE (1+x)f'(x) = αf(x) with f(0) = 1 uniquely determines f(x) = (1+x)^α. The coefficient recurrence that follows from this ODE is the key to all identities in the file. Mathlib's HasFPowerSeriesOnBall provides the analyticity framework.
mathContext: The ODE $(1+x)f'(x) = \alpha f(x)$ with $f(0) = 1$ has unique solution $f(x) = (1+x)^\alpha$. At the coefficient level: $(k+1)C(\alpha, k+1) + kC(\alpha, k) = \alpha C(\alpha, k)$.

title: ODE Recurrence and Coefficient Uniqueness
content: The ODE recurrence (k+1)·C(α,k+1) = (α-k)·C(α,k) is proved directly from the falling factorial definition using field_simp. The uniqueness theorem genBinom_unique_from_ode shows any sequence satisfying this recurrence with a₀ = 1 must equal genBinom. The proof uses induction with mul_left_cancel₀ on the nonzero factor (k+1), which is the discrete analogue of ODE uniqueness (Picard-Lindelöf).
mathContext: $(k+1)\binom{\alpha}{k+1} = (\alpha - k)\binom{\alpha}{k}$ uniquely determines $\binom{\alpha}{k}$ from $\binom{\alpha}{0} = 1$. This is the Lean proof of the coefficient-level ODE identity.

title: Analyticity from Mathlib
content: The generalized binomial series is analytic on the open unit ball, established directly from Mathlib's Real.one_add_rpow_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero. This single line provides the entire analytic framework — HasFPowerSeriesOnBall encodes convergence, uniqueness of coefficients, and validity of term-by-term operations.
mathContext: $(1+y)^\alpha$ has the formal power series `binomialSeries ℝ α` on the ball $|y| < 1$. The `HasFPowerSeriesOnBall` type packages convergence, representation, and analyticity.

title: Functional Equation
content: The functional equation (1+x)^α · (1+x)^β = (1+x)^(α+β) follows from Mathlib's rpow_add, which requires 1+x > 0 (i.e., x > -1). The special cases (1+x)^0 = 1 and (1+x)^1 = 1+x establish the group structure of real powers.
mathContext: $(1+x)^\alpha \cdot (1+x)^\beta = (1+x)^{\alpha+\beta}$ for $x > -1$. This is the multiplicative version of the additive identity $\alpha + \beta$ in the exponent.

title: Absorption Identity (Derivative Correspondence)
content: The absorption identity α·C(α-1,k) = (k+1)·C(α,k+1) is the most significant new result. Analytically, it encodes the derivative formula d/dx[(1+x)^α] = α(1+x)^(α-1) at the coefficient level: the k-th coefficient of the derivative series (k+1)·C(α,k+1) equals α times the k-th coefficient C(α-1,k) of (1+x)^(α-1). The proof uses induction on k, applying the ODE recurrence for both α and α-1 in the inductive step, followed by field_simp and ring.

title: Half-Integer Binomial Coefficients and the Square Root Series
content: Explicit computation of C(1/2, k) for k = 0,1,2,3 gives the first terms of √(1+x) = 1 + x/2 - x²/8 + x³/16 - ···. The alternating signs for k ≥ 2 reflect the concavity of the square root function. The theorem genBinom_half_ne_zero proves all C(1/2,k) are nonzero by induction: if C(1/2,k+1) = 0, the ODE recurrence forces (1/2-k)·C(1/2,k) = 0, but C(1/2,k) ≠ 0 by the IH and 1/2-k ≠ 0 since 2k ≠ 1 (omega).
mathContext: $\binom{1/2}{0} = 1$, $\binom{1/2}{1} = 1/2$, $\binom{1/2}{2} = -1/8$, $\binom{1/2}{3} = 1/16$. All $\binom{1/2}{k} \neq 0$ because $1/2 \notin \mathbb{N}$ means no factor $(1/2 - i)$ in the falling product vanishes.
